html:
For the past two years I’ve been trying my hand at podcasting. The conversations are a blast; the editing can drive you up the wall. Recently a friend and I started experimenting with AI-assisted editing, and along the way I wrote this short piece about the audio processing side of things.

If you’d like to hear more about the technology behind podcast editing, or about the little AI tool we built, let us know in the comments. We may write more on the subject, and we might even open-source the tool.

The three of us recorded an episode, each on our own phone. At one point the guest talks about a show where they had rented two rows of lights and ended up using neither of them. Listen on headphones and something about that sentence is off. Both times he says deng (灯, “light”), the word is almost over, yet a faint low hum is still trailing along behind it.

When it was my turn to ask a question, the problem was a different kind of ugly. My voice was loud enough, but the syllables ran into one another and smeared. Turning the headphones up a notch didn’t help; it was still mushy, and as soon as the guest replied you had to turn them back down.

Had we not started recording yet, I would have asked everyone to talk for ten seconds at their normal volume while I listened on headphones. Anyone who sounded as if they were sitting on the far side of the room would move their phone a little closer and try again. But this episode was already in the can. How much of it could we still save?

Each of the three short clips below plays the same sentence twice, before and after. The two versions are loudness-matched, so you can leave the volume alone while you listen.

First, the tail on “deng”

Starts at 0 s in the clip. A is the first low-frequency fix; B also pulls down the low-frequency tail (from 4.83 s).

We had already taken one pass at the hum. In the guest’s voice we had found a prominent low-frequency bump around 130 Hz and brought it down a little. The catch is that part of what gives a male voice its weight also lives in that region. Keep cutting across the board and you may end up with the hum still there and the voice gone thin.

On the second pass we listened only for the moment when a syllable dies away. While he is saying deng, the vowel is left to ring out in full. Only once the speech in the midrange has decayed, while the low end underneath is still sounding, do we pull that band down a little further. The figure looks at the same 105–150 Hz band: it is reduced by about 5 dB during ordinary speech and by about 9 dB at word endings like this one. These are medians measured over many passages of the guest’s speech. Listen to the two deng again: as he opens the word his voice still has its body, and at the end the hum clears away a little faster.

Make “shiqing” clear without making “shi” sting

Starts at 10 s in the clip. A is the natural, carefully edited version; B adds the full voice-enhancement chain (from 16.38 s).

I asked the guest why he feels that doing physics is, in its way, an emotional pursuit. The word shiqing (事情, “thing” or “matter”) comes up twice in that sentence, which makes it ideal material for tuning the timbre. I listen first to the fricative hiss at the start of shi, then to the vowel that follows it. If that hiss is too weak, the syllables tend to glue together into a lump. But if all you do is brighten everything, every shi becomes clear, and every shi also stings.

The voice on this phone recording sounds a little boxy around 500 Hz. We used an equalizer to pull that region down gently and lift the area around 3 kHz a touch, so the consonant onsets come forward. A few shi still sounded harsh. For those especially loud high-frequency fricatives, we let a de-esser clamp down briefly. The other host’s consonants were already clear, so his upper midrange got only a slight lift.

With the whole enhancement chain in place, the consonant onsets were much clearer. Just from listening to the before and after, though, you can’t tell how much of that is down to the EQ and how much to the de-esser.

When the guest leans on a word, should we ride the fader for him?

Starts at 23 s in the clip. A has the broadband compressor switched off; B has it switched on (from 28.82 s).

The guest says “zai Zhongguo, keyi zheme shuo ba” (“in China, you could put it that way”), and Zhongguo (中国, “China”) comes out noticeably louder than the “keyi zheme shuo ba” that follows. Turn the whole sentence down and the second half suffers as well. We wanted to keep the punch in the way he speaks and rein him in just a little when he gets especially loud. The tool for that is a compressor.

If you were riding the level by hand, you would probably pull the fader down a bit on the stressed word and then ease it back up once he got quieter. A compressor does exactly that for you. We used it very lightly in this episode: a steady vowel that sits 6 dB above the threshold still sits about 4 dB above it after processing. How much a single short syllable actually gets reduced depends on whether the fader can move fast enough to catch it.

Look at the first deep dip in the green line. Around Zhongguo, the gain briefly drops by about 3 dB. The line falls quickly and climbs back much more slowly. Here the attack time is set to 19 ms and the release time to 155 ms, so even after the stressed word has passed, the fader takes a moment to return to where it was. We matched the loudness of the whole sentence with the compressor on and off and listened again. With compression, Zhongguo is still where the stress falls in the sentence; it just doesn’t jump out at you as much.

Once the three of us start trading lines, there is another round of listening to do. First we found passages where each person speaks on their own and brought their levels close together. Then we went back to the questions and answers, and only at the very end did we add the music. Measured on the exported MP3, the whole episode comes in at an integrated loudness of about −16 LUFS. When someone else starts talking, you can finally keep your hand off the volume button.

As for that deng: loop it ten times on its own and you can still pick holes in it. I would rather put it back between the sentences on either side and listen to it there. The guest’s voice is still recognizably his, and I finally have the headspace to wonder why those two rows of lights never got used. That is where the edit can stop.

Further reading

From the Ziyu Acoustics archive: “What on earth is a decibel (dB), and why 1 + 1 ≠ 2”

Giannoulis et al., “Digital dynamic range compressor design: A tutorial and analysis” (AES, 2012)
